title: Money
blurb: How money works, budgeting, compound interest and investing basics.

lessons.title: How money works
lessons.summary: What money is and where it comes from.

cards.title: What money does
cards.text: Money has three jobs: a medium of exchange (you can buy with it), a unit of account (prices are measured in it) and a store of value (it keeps worth over time).

cards.title: From barter to apps
cards.text: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: you must find someone who has what you want and wants what you have. Money solved that.

cards.title: Fiat money
cards.text: Euro notes aren't backed by gold. Their value comes from trust and from law: governments accept them for taxes and require them to be accepted for debts.

cards.title: Most money is digital
cards.text: Physical notes and coins are a small part of the money supply. Most money exists as numbers in bank accounts, created when banks lend.

cards.title: Central banks
cards.text: The European Central Bank sets interest rates for the euro area, aiming for inflation close to 2% a year. Banco de Portugal is part of this system.

cards.title: Inflation

viz.unit: price of a basket, € (2% a year)

cards.text: Inflation means prices rise over time, so each euro buys less. At 2% a year, prices double in about 35 years.

cards.title: The rule of 72
cards.text: Divide 72 by an annual percentage rate to estimate how many years it takes for something to double. It works for prices, savings and debts.

cards.title: Interest
cards.text: Interest is the price of money. Borrowers pay it; savers earn it. Higher central bank rates usually mean pricier loans and better savings rates.

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.text: Prices rise when many people want something scarce, and fall when it's plentiful or unwanted. Concert tickets and summer flights are classic examples.

cards.title: Inflation eats cash
cards.text: €10,000 kept under the mattress for 10 years with 3% inflation would buy what about €7,400 buys today.

quiz.q: Roughly how long does it take for prices to double at 2% inflation?

cards.title: Pay yourself first
cards.text: Move savings out as soon as your salary arrives, not with what's left at the end of the month; there's rarely anything left.

cards.title: The 50/30/20 rule
cards.text: A simple starting split of take-home pay: 50% on needs, 30% on wants and 20% on savings or paying off debt. Adjust to your situation.

cards.title: Needs vs wants

items.b: need, but the latest model is a want

cards.text: Needs are things you must pay for (rent, food, transport, bills). Wants make life nicer but are optional. Many things have a need part and a want part.

cards.title: Emergency fund
cards.text: Keep three to six months of essential expenses in an easy-access savings account. It turns a crisis, like losing a job or a broken car, into an inconvenience.

cards.title: Track first
cards.text: Most people underestimate small, frequent spending. Track every expense for one month before making a budget; the results usually surprise.

cards.title: Subscriptions creep
cards.text: Streaming, apps, gym and cloud storage: €8 here, €12 there, and you may be paying for things you don't use. Check bank statements and cancel what you've forgotten.

cards.title: The latte factor, in perspective
cards.text: Small daily savings add up, but big decisions, such as rent, car and housing, matter more. Optimise the big three before agonising over a coffee.

cards.title: Mental accounting

items.w: "It's a bonus, so I can blow it"
items.r: "A euro is a euro: does this fit my plan?"

cards.text: We treat money differently depending on where it came from: a tax refund feels like "free money" and gets spent. A euro is a euro wherever it comes from.

cards.title: Lifestyle inflation
cards.text: When pay rises, spending tends to rise to match it. Saving half of every raise keeps your lifestyle growing while your savings grow faster.

cards.title: A simple budget
cards.text: Take-home pay €1,600. Needs €800, wants €480, savings €320. After six months, €1,920 saved: a start on an emergency fund.

quiz.q: How big should an emergency fund usually be?

cards.title: Simple vs compound
cards.text: Simple interest pays only on what you put in. Compound interest also pays on past interest, so growth speeds up over time.

cards.title: The formula
cards.text: After n years, money grows by the factor (1 + r) for each year. Small differences in r or n make huge differences.

cards.title: €1,000 at 5%
cards.text: After 10 years: €1,629. After 20: €2,653. After 40: €7,040. Most of the growth comes late.

cards.title: Time beats amount
cards.text: Starting early matters more than investing a lot. Someone who invests from 25 to 35 and stops can end up with more than someone who invests from 35 to 65, at the same return.

cards.title: Compounding debt
cards.text: Compounding works against you on debt. Credit card balances can charge 15–20% a year or more, doubling in about four or five years if unpaid.

cards.title: Fees matter
cards.text: A 1% yearly fee sounds tiny but compounds too. Over 30 years it can eat about a quarter of your final pot.

cards.title: Nominal vs real
cards.text: A 5% return with 3% inflation is only about 2% of real growth in buying power. Always compare returns with inflation.

cards.title: Einstein's quote?

items.w: Einstein called it the eighth wonder
items.r: No evidence he ever said it

cards.text: "Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world" is often credited to Einstein, but there's no evidence he said it. The maths is real either way.

cards.title: Regular contributions

steps: Buys more when prices are low

cards.text: Adding a fixed amount every month, rather than one lump, smooths the ups and downs of markets. It's called euro-cost averaging.

cards.title: €100 a month
cards.text: Investing €100 a month at 5% a year for 30 years: you pay in €36,000, and it grows to about €83,000.

quiz.q: What makes compound interest different from simple interest?
options: It earns interest on past interest

quiz.q: Using the rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 6%?

cards.title: Saving vs investing
cards.text: Saving keeps money safe for the short term. Investing buys assets that can grow over the long term, with the risk of falling in value along the way.

cards.title: Shares
cards.text: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. You can gain if its price rises and if it pays dividends, and you can lose if it falls.

cards.title: Bonds
cards.text: A bond is a loan to a government or company. They pay you interest and return the money at the end. Usually steadier than shares, with lower long-term returns.

cards.title: Risk and return
cards.text: Higher expected returns come with bigger swings. There's no reliable way to get high returns without accepting risk.

cards.title: Diversification
cards.text: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. Spreading money across many companies, countries and asset types reduces the damage any single failure can do.

cards.title: Index funds
cards.text: An index fund buys every company in an index, like the S&P 500 or a world index, at very low cost. Most actively managed funds fail to beat their index over long periods.

cards.title: Time in the market

items.r: Time in the market beats timing the market

cards.text: Markets fall often, sometimes sharply, but have historically recovered and grown over long periods. Missing just the best few days can badly hurt returns.

cards.title: Too good to be true
cards.text: Promises of high guaranteed returns are a red flag. If it's guaranteed, it's low; if it's high, it isn't guaranteed. Scams often push urgency and secrecy.

cards.title: Emotions and investing
cards.text: Fear makes people sell after crashes and greed makes them buy at peaks: the opposite of "buy low, sell high". A written plan helps you stick to your course.

cards.title: Before you invest
cards.text: A common order: clear expensive debt, build an emergency fund, then invest money you won't need for at least five years. This is general information, not personal advice.

options: To reduce the damage of any single failure
quiz.explain: Don't put all eggs in one basket.

cards.title: GDP
cards.text: Gross domestic product is the total value of goods and services a country produces in a year. It measures the size of an economy, not its wellbeing.

cards.title: Recession
cards.text: A recession is a significant fall in economic activity, often defined as two quarters in a row of falling GDP. Jobs and incomes usually suffer.

cards.title: Opportunity cost
cards.text: The real cost of something is what you give up to get it. An evening studying costs the evening out you didn't have.

cards.title: Incentives
cards.text: People respond to incentives. Taxes on sugary drinks reduce sales; deposits on bottles increase recycling. Badly designed ones backfire.

cards.title: Comparative advantage
cards.text: Countries gain by specialising in what they're relatively best at and trading, even if one is better at everything. Portugal and England's wine and cloth was Ricardo's 1817 example.

cards.title: Tragedy of the commons
cards.text: When a shared resource is free for all, everyone overuses it. Overfishing is a classic example; quotas and ownership rules can help.

cards.title: Taxes
cards.text: Taxes fund public services. Portugal uses income tax (IRS) with rates that rise with income, VAT (IVA) on purchases at 23% standard in the mainland, and social security contributions.

cards.title: Unemployment
cards.text: Some unemployment is normal as people change jobs. The rate is the share of people who want work and are looking for it but don't have it.

cards.title: Exchange rates
cards.text: Exchange rates are the price of one currency in another. A stronger euro makes holidays abroad cheaper but Portuguese exports pricier for foreigners.

cards.title: Reading a headline

items.w: Inflation fell, so prices are lower
items.r: Prices still rose, just more slowly

cards.text: "Inflation falls to 2%" doesn't mean prices fell; it means they are rising more slowly. Only negative inflation, called deflation, means prices fall.
